newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnia banks need serious reforms - World Bank.
newsitem.headline: Bosnia banks need serious reforms - World Bank.

text.p: Sweeping reforms are needed to cure Bosnia's ailing banks but the biggest challenge will be winning back the confidence of depositors and investors who lost their savings during Yugoslavia's bloody disintegration, a World Bank official said on Thursday.

"Banks face very serious difficulties in this country and it is, above all, a crisis of confidence in the banking system," the World Bank's deputy mission director, Saumya Mitra, told Bosnian bankers at a financial forum in Sarajevo.
Fifty-three banks operate in peacetime Bosnia, with 23 state or socially-owned accounting for up to 95 percent of total assets -- estimated at 8.6 billion German Marks ($6 billion).
A recent World Bank study said that 90 percent of the banking system's total assets are non-performing, putting the actual value of assets at 1.1 billion marks or a mere 21 million per bank.

More than half of the country's banks are newly formed private banks with small net capital and limited experience. The private banks make their living mainly through off-balance sheet activities such as transfers and foreign exchange trading.

Bosnians lost some four billion marks when their foreign currency savings were frozen with the outbreak of fighting in old Yugoslavia in 1991. Most people now keep their cash safely stashed away at home.

The country owes three billion marks to creditors in the Paris and London clubs as well as other international financial institutions. One billion in local currency-denominated assets were lost to hyperinflation and war.
Talks with London creditors began on Wednesday and are expected to allow a 90 percent forgiveness and restructuring of the remaining debt, foreign experts said.
To help cure the crisis of confidence, the World Bank proposed a set of measures to get banks back on track.
Mitra said the country needs to set up effective banking supervision and licencing and said that the Moslem-Croat federation's banking agency has been functioning well.
The Serb part of the country has yet to establish such an agency, the bank study reported.

"A further condition relates to ownership, governance and management of banks. Decisions have to be taken in a transparent manner on purely banking and commercial criteria and not on political or any other criteria," he said.
In former Yugoslavia, big enterprises would help set up a bank and then receive loans on favorable terms, eventually pushing the banks into insolvency.
Mitra called for special efforts to clean up bank balance sheets to gain the trust of depositors.

Privatisation is expected to offer some relief when citizens are given certificates for their hard-currency savings which will buy off some of their claims. The certificates could be used to purchase shares in companies or buy socially-owned flats.
"But confidence in the banking system would also be improved if there was a system of deposit preference which would lead at some stage to a form of deposit insurance," Mitra said.
Banking reforms were likely to hurt state-owned giants the most but a change of management and downsizing were inevitable.

"Times of change...create uncertainty and they create anxiety amongst people working in banks but there is no doubting the fact that there is an urgent need for restructuring and privatisation," Mitra said.
"Without speedy privatisation the progress that we have seen in the last year may be put in jeopardy."
